Melanotic neuroectodermal tumor of infancy Melanotic neuroectodermal tumor of infancy (MNTI) is a rare, typically benign neoplasm almost exclusively affecting infants younger than 1 year, with a median age at diagnosis being 5 months. Historically termedmelanotic progonoma, this entity has been described in fewer than 500 cases in the literature.1,2More than 90% of cases involve the head and neck, most commonly the maxilla (60%-80%). Other affected sites include the skull, mandible, and less frequently, intracranial and extracraniofacial locations such as the epididymis, ovaries, and bones of the extremities.1-3Clinically, MNTI presents as a rapidly enlarging, firm, nontender mass, often pigmented due to melanin, though nonpigmented forms occur.2,4,5Presentation varies by site; maxillary tumors may interfere with feeding or displace teeth, while intracranial lesions can cause neurologic symptoms or raised intracranial pressure.3,6Mandibular lesions may cause pathologic fracture.1 CT typically shows a lytic, expansile lesion with enhancing soft tissue and, less commonly, a sunburst periosteal reaction, which is more frequent in calvarial than maxillary MNTIs.3,4,7MRI adds detail on soft tissue and melanin-related T1 signal changes (Figure 2). Diffusion restriction is usually present due to the high tumor cellularity.4T1 hyperintensity is quite specific for MNTI but lacks sensitivity, as not all cases show this feature.7Key differential includes neuroblastoma—another neuroectodermal tumor—which may show heterogeneous enhancement with calcifications and can metastasize to the orbit. Abdominal imaging (CT or ultrasonography) can help identify the primary site. Furthermore, although both entities may be associated with elevated urinary vanillylmandelic acid levels, only neuroblastoma typically demonstrates uptake on a meta-iodobenzylguanidine scan.8Other differentials include Ewing sarcoma, characterized by permeative lysis and aggressive periosteal reaction, but a disease of older children; while Langerhans cell histiocytosis typically presents as a punched-out lytic lesion with an associated soft tissue component in untreated cases and often lacks a periosteal reaction.9Histologically, MNTI shows a biphasic pattern (hallmark of the tumor) with large, melanin-rich epithelioid cells at the periphery and small, primitive neurogenic cells centrally, arranged in nests, cords, or pseudoalveolar structures within fibrocollagenous stroma.2,6Atypia, necrosis, and mitotic activity are generally absent.3On immunohistochemistry, large cells are positive for pan-cytokeratin, epithelial membrane antigen, vimentin, and HMB-45; small cells stain, with neuron specific enolase, synaptophysin, and chromogranin. S100 is usually negative5,10Although definitive diagnosis requires biopsy,10imaging features combined with awareness of the typical age group can strongly suggest the diagnosis. Surgical excision with clear margins is the mainstay of treatment.1Complete resection may be limited by proximity to vital structures, especially in infants.2While less aggressive surgery may suffice in select cases, recurrence risk supports efforts at total removal. Adjuvant therapy is reserved for incomplete resection or aggressive disease; chemotherapy may be effective but lacks definitive outcome data.1,7Despite its benign nature, MNTI has a significant recurrence rate (10%-45%), usually within 1 to 2 years postsurgery.2Risk factors include early age, large tumor size, incomplete excision, and nonmaxillary sites. Malignant transformation and metastasis are rare but reported.2 Close follow-up is essential due to recurrence risk.5Surveillance typically includes clinical exams and MRI at regular intervals for early detection.2,6Long-term monitoring is advised to address late recurrence or treatment-related complications.5

Melanotic neuroectodermal tumor of infancy Melanotic neuroectodermal tumor of infancy (MNTI) is a rare, typically benign neoplasm almost exclusively affecting infants younger than 1 year, with a median age at diagnosis being 5 months. Historically termedmelanotic progonoma, this entity has been described in fewer than 500 cases in the literature.1,2More than 90% of cases involve the head and neck, most commonly the maxilla (60%-80%). Other affected sites include the skull, mandible, and less frequently, intracranial and extracraniofacial locations such as the epididymis, ovaries, and bones of the extremities.1-3Clinically, MNTI presents as a rapidly enlarging, firm, nontender mass, often pigmented due to melanin, though nonpigmented forms occur.2,4,5Presentation varies by site; maxillary tumors may interfere with feeding or displace teeth, while intracranial lesions can cause neurologic symptoms or raised intracranial pressure.3,6Mandibular lesions may cause pathologic fracture.1 CT typically shows a lytic, expansile lesion with enhancing soft tissue and, less commonly, a sunburst periosteal reaction, which is more frequent in calvarial than maxillary MNTIs.3,4,7MRI adds detail on soft tissue and melanin-related T1 signal changes (Figure 2). Diffusion restriction is usually present due to the high tumor cellularity.4T1 hyperintensity is quite specific for MNTI but lacks sensitivity, as not all cases show this feature.7Key differential includes neuroblastoma—another neuroectodermal tumor—which may show heterogeneous enhancement with calcifications and can metastasize to the orbit. Abdominal imaging (CT or ultrasonography) can help identify the primary site. Furthermore, although both entities may be associated with elevated urinary vanillylmandelic acid levels, only neuroblastoma typically demonstrates uptake on a meta-iodobenzylguanidine scan.8Other differentials include Ewing sarcoma, characterized by permeative lysis and aggressive periosteal reaction, but a disease of older children; while Langerhans cell histiocytosis typically presents as a punched-out lytic lesion with an associated soft tissue component in untreated cases and often lacks a periosteal reaction.9Histologically, MNTI shows a biphasic pattern (hallmark of the tumor) with large, melanin-rich epithelioid cells at the periphery and small, primitive neurogenic cells centrally, arranged in nests, cords, or pseudoalveolar structures within fibrocollagenous stroma.2,6Atypia, necrosis, and mitotic activity are generally absent.3On immunohistochemistry, large cells are positive for pan-cytokeratin, epithelial membrane antigen, vimentin, and HMB-45; small cells stain, with neuron specific enolase, synaptophysin, and chromogranin. S100 is usually negative5,10Although definitive diagnosis requires biopsy,10imaging features combined with awareness of the typical age group can strongly suggest the diagnosis. Surgical excision with clear margins is the mainstay of treatment.1Complete resection may be limited by proximity to vital structures, especially in infants.2While less aggressive surgery may suffice in select cases, recurrence risk supports efforts at total removal. Adjuvant therapy is reserved for incomplete resection or aggressive disease; chemotherapy may be effective but lacks definitive outcome data.1,7Despite its benign nature, MNTI has a significant recurrence rate (10%-45%), usually within 1 to 2 years postsurgery.2Risk factors include early age, large tumor size, incomplete excision, and nonmaxillary sites. Malignant transformation and metastasis are rare but reported.2 Close follow-up is essential due to recurrence risk.5Surveillance typically includes clinical exams and MRI at regular intervals for early detection.2,6Long-term monitoring is advised to address late recurrence or treatment-related complications.5

Melanotic neuroectodermal tumor of infancy Melanotic neuroectodermal tumor of infancy (MNTI) is a rare, typically benign neoplasm almost exclusively affecting infants younger than 1 year, with a median age at diagnosis being 5 months. Historically termedmelanotic progonoma, this entity has been described in fewer than 500 cases in the literature.1,2More than 90% of cases involve the head and neck, most commonly the maxilla (60%-80%). Other affected sites include the skull, mandible, and less frequently, intracranial and extracraniofacial locations such as the epididymis, ovaries, and bones of the extremities.1-3Clinically, MNTI presents as a rapidly enlarging, firm, nontender mass, often pigmented due to melanin, though nonpigmented forms occur.2,4,5Presentation varies by site; maxillary tumors may interfere with feeding or displace teeth, while intracranial lesions can cause neurologic symptoms or raised intracranial pressure.3,6Mandibular lesions may cause pathologic fracture.1 CT typically shows a lytic, expansile lesion with enhancing soft tissue and, less commonly, a sunburst periosteal reaction, which is more frequent in calvarial than maxillary MNTIs.3,4,7MRI adds detail on soft tissue and melanin-related T1 signal changes (Figure 2). Diffusion restriction is usually present due to the high tumor cellularity.4T1 hyperintensity is quite specific for MNTI but lacks sensitivity, as not all cases show this feature.7Key differential includes neuroblastoma—another neuroectodermal tumor—which may show heterogeneous enhancement with calcifications and can metastasize to the orbit. Abdominal imaging (CT or ultrasonography) can help identify the primary site. Furthermore, although both entities may be associated with elevated urinary vanillylmandelic acid levels, only neuroblastoma typically demonstrates uptake on a meta-iodobenzylguanidine scan.8Other differentials include Ewing sarcoma, characterized by permeative lysis and aggressive periosteal reaction, but a disease of older children; while Langerhans cell histiocytosis typically presents as a punched-out lytic lesion with an associated soft tissue component in untreated cases and often lacks a periosteal reaction.9Histologically, MNTI shows a biphasic pattern (hallmark of the tumor) with large, melanin-rich epithelioid cells at the periphery and small, primitive neurogenic cells centrally, arranged in nests, cords, or pseudoalveolar structures within fibrocollagenous stroma.2,6Atypia, necrosis, and mitotic activity are generally absent.3On immunohistochemistry, large cells are positive for pan-cytokeratin, epithelial membrane antigen, vimentin, and HMB-45; small cells stain, with neuron specific enolase, synaptophysin, and chromogranin. S100 is usually negative5,10Although definitive diagnosis requires biopsy,10imaging features combined with awareness of the typical age group can strongly suggest the diagnosis. Surgical excision with clear margins is the mainstay of treatment.1Complete resection may be limited by proximity to vital structures, especially in infants.2While less aggressive surgery may suffice in select cases, recurrence risk supports efforts at total removal. Adjuvant therapy is reserved for incomplete resection or aggressive disease; chemotherapy may be effective but lacks definitive outcome data.1,7Despite its benign nature, MNTI has a significant recurrence rate (10%-45%), usually within 1 to 2 years postsurgery.2Risk factors include early age, large tumor size, incomplete excision, and nonmaxillary sites. Malignant transformation and metastasis are rare but reported.2 Close follow-up is essential due to recurrence risk.5Surveillance typically includes clinical exams and MRI at regular intervals for early detection.2,6Long-term monitoring is advised to address late recurrence or treatment-related complications.5

Melanotic neuroectodermal tumor of infancy Melanotic neuroectodermal tumor of infancy (MNTI) is a rare, typically benign neoplasm almost exclusively affecting infants younger than 1 year, with a median age at diagnosis being 5 months. Historically termedmelanotic progonoma, this entity has been described in fewer than 500 cases in the literature.1,2More than 90% of cases involve the head and neck, most commonly the maxilla (60%-80%). Other affected sites include the skull, mandible, and less frequently, intracranial and extracraniofacial locations such as the epididymis, ovaries, and bones of the extremities.1-3Clinically, MNTI presents as a rapidly enlarging, firm, nontender mass, often pigmented due to melanin, though nonpigmented forms occur.2,4,5Presentation varies by site; maxillary tumors may interfere with feeding or displace teeth, while intracranial lesions can cause neurologic symptoms or raised intracranial pressure.3,6Mandibular lesions may cause pathologic fracture.1 CT typically shows a lytic, expansile lesion with enhancing soft tissue and, less commonly, a sunburst periosteal reaction, which is more frequent in calvarial than maxillary MNTIs.3,4,7MRI adds detail on soft tissue and melanin-related T1 signal changes (Figure 2). Diffusion restriction is usually present due to the high tumor cellularity.4T1 hyperintensity is quite specific for MNTI but lacks sensitivity, as not all cases show this feature.7Key differential includes neuroblastoma—another neuroectodermal tumor—which may show heterogeneous enhancement with calcifications and can metastasize to the orbit. Abdominal imaging (CT or ultrasonography) can help identify the primary site. Furthermore, although both entities may be associated with elevated urinary vanillylmandelic acid levels, only neuroblastoma typically demonstrates uptake on a meta-iodobenzylguanidine scan.8Other differentials include Ewing sarcoma, characterized by permeative lysis and aggressive periosteal reaction, but a disease of older children; while Langerhans cell histiocytosis typically presents as a punched-out lytic lesion with an associated soft tissue component in untreated cases and often lacks a periosteal reaction.9Histologically, MNTI shows a biphasic pattern (hallmark of the tumor) with large, melanin-rich epithelioid cells at the periphery and small, primitive neurogenic cells centrally, arranged in nests, cords, or pseudoalveolar structures within fibrocollagenous stroma.2,6Atypia, necrosis, and mitotic activity are generally absent.3On immunohistochemistry, large cells are positive for pan-cytokeratin, epithelial membrane antigen, vimentin, and HMB-45; small cells stain, with neuron specific enolase, synaptophysin, and chromogranin. S100 is usually negative5,10Although definitive diagnosis requires biopsy,10imaging features combined with awareness of the typical age group can strongly suggest the diagnosis. Surgical excision with clear margins is the mainstay of treatment.1Complete resection may be limited by proximity to vital structures, especially in infants.2While less aggressive surgery may suffice in select cases, recurrence risk supports efforts at total removal. Adjuvant therapy is reserved for incomplete resection or aggressive disease; chemotherapy may be effective but lacks definitive outcome data.1,7Despite its benign nature, MNTI has a significant recurrence rate (10%-45%), usually within 1 to 2 years postsurgery.2Risk factors include early age, large tumor size, incomplete excision, and nonmaxillary sites. Malignant transformation and metastasis are rare but reported.2 Close follow-up is essential due to recurrence risk.5Surveillance typically includes clinical exams and MRI at regular intervals for early detection.2,6Long-term monitoring is advised to address late recurrence or treatment-related complications.5

Melanotic neuroectodermal tumor of infancy Melanotic neuroectodermal tumor of infancy (MNTI) is a rare, typically benign neoplasm almost exclusively affecting infants younger than 1 year, with a median age at diagnosis being 5 months. Historically termedmelanotic progonoma, this entity has been described in fewer than 500 cases in the literature.1,2More than 90% of cases involve the head and neck, most commonly the maxilla (60%-80%). Other affected sites include the skull, mandible, and less frequently, intracranial and extracraniofacial locations such as the epididymis, ovaries, and bones of the extremities.1-3Clinically, MNTI presents as a rapidly enlarging, firm, nontender mass, often pigmented due to melanin, though nonpigmented forms occur.2,4,5Presentation varies by site; maxillary tumors may interfere with feeding or displace teeth, while intracranial lesions can cause neurologic symptoms or raised intracranial pressure.3,6Mandibular lesions may cause pathologic fracture.1 CT typically shows a lytic, expansile lesion with enhancing soft tissue and, less commonly, a sunburst periosteal reaction, which is more frequent in calvarial than maxillary MNTIs.3,4,7MRI adds detail on soft tissue and melanin-related T1 signal changes (Figure 2). Diffusion restriction is usually present due to the high tumor cellularity.4T1 hyperintensity is quite specific for MNTI but lacks sensitivity, as not all cases show this feature.7Key differential includes neuroblastoma—another neuroectodermal tumor—which may show heterogeneous enhancement with calcifications and can metastasize to the orbit. Abdominal imaging (CT or ultrasonography) can help identify the primary site. Furthermore, although both entities may be associated with elevated urinary vanillylmandelic acid levels, only neuroblastoma typically demonstrates uptake on a meta-iodobenzylguanidine scan.8Other differentials include Ewing sarcoma, characterized by permeative lysis and aggressive periosteal reaction, but a disease of older children; while Langerhans cell histiocytosis typically presents as a punched-out lytic lesion with an associated soft tissue component in untreated cases and often lacks a periosteal reaction.9Histologically, MNTI shows a biphasic pattern (hallmark of the tumor) with large, melanin-rich epithelioid cells at the periphery and small, primitive neurogenic cells centrally, arranged in nests, cords, or pseudoalveolar structures within fibrocollagenous stroma.2,6Atypia, necrosis, and mitotic activity are generally absent.3On immunohistochemistry, large cells are positive for pan-cytokeratin, epithelial membrane antigen, vimentin, and HMB-45; small cells stain, with neuron specific enolase, synaptophysin, and chromogranin. S100 is usually negative5,10Although definitive diagnosis requires biopsy,10imaging features combined with awareness of the typical age group can strongly suggest the diagnosis. Surgical excision with clear margins is the mainstay of treatment.1Complete resection may be limited by proximity to vital structures, especially in infants.2While less aggressive surgery may suffice in select cases, recurrence risk supports efforts at total removal. Adjuvant therapy is reserved for incomplete resection or aggressive disease; chemotherapy may be effective but lacks definitive outcome data.1,7Despite its benign nature, MNTI has a significant recurrence rate (10%-45%), usually within 1 to 2 years postsurgery.2Risk factors include early age, large tumor size, incomplete excision, and nonmaxillary sites. Malignant transformation and metastasis are rare but reported.2 Close follow-up is essential due to recurrence risk.5Surveillance typically includes clinical exams and MRI at regular intervals for early detection.2,6Long-term monitoring is advised to address late recurrence or treatment-related complications.5
